papers.title: Using the aperiodic slope across learning to predict sleep-based memory consolidation
papers.abstract: Homeostatic mechanisms adjust synaptic strengths to regulate neuronal activity across wake-sleep cycles. Although sleep supports memory consolidation, limited research has explored how sleep-induced homeostatic changes influence memory outcomes in humans. The EEG-derived aperiodic slope (1/f) could be a candidate measure of homeostatic memory processes through its reflection of neural excitation-inhibition balance. In this study, 27 participants learned object-word pairs, and completed an immediate recognition test before either a nap or equivalent wakeful period. Resting-state EEG was recorded, both before and after learning and the interval, to derive changes in aperiodic slope values. A delayed recognition test then assessed whether changes in the aperiodic slope (i.e., homeostatic activity) across learning and the interval predicted memory accuracy and N400 amplitude, an index of stimulus expectancy and recognition. Our study found evidence to suggest homeostatic renormalisation, for the nap condition only, indicated by a shift towards inhibition across sleep which was inversely related to the slope change across learning. Although the aperiodic slope change across the nap and wake intervals did not predict delayed memory accuracy, a shift towards inhibition during learning was beneficial for memory accuracy, only in the nap condition. Similarly, a shift towards inhibition across learning, followed by a shift towards excitation in the nap condition, predicted reduced N400 amplitudes. This suggests that homeostatic renormalisation across the nap influenced model updating and stimulus expectancy. This study provides evidence for a link between synaptic homeostatic processes and memory consolidation, emphasising the importance of encoding-related aperiodic activity in this relationship.

papers.title: Identifying Network Factors Driving Changes in Brain Connectivity During Aging via Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models
papers.abstract: Brain network organization emerges from ongoing network dynamics that continuously create, maintain, and reorganize connectivity patterns. At both the structural and functional levels, these dynamics shape network evolution throughout the lifespan. Here, we introduce a data-driven framework based on Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models (SAOMs), which model longitudinal network changes as a process of local edge formation and dissolution driven by local-connectivity factors. Applied to functional and structural brain networks from an aging cohort, the resulting models recovered a set of interacting mechanisms that collectively promote hub formation, short-range connectivity, and modular organization. These factors were derived through a novel data-driven factor-selection procedure rather than specified a priori, allowing network mechanisms underlying longitudinal change to be identified directly from observations. Functional networks exhibited substantially higher rates of change than structural networks, suggesting more frequent opportunities for network maintenance and reorganization. Structural networks additionally showed despecification in the hub-forming mechanisms with cognitive impairment. These results support a view of brain network organization as an actively maintained process emerging from ongoing local connectivity dynamics. More broadly, this framework provides a general approach for studying longitudinal network dynamics through the estimation of network-generating mechanisms over time.

papers.title: Inferotemporal cortex stimulation is perceived before its onset
papers.abstract: Neural response latency measures when stimulus-evoked activity becomes detectable, but it does not reveal when the brain assigns the causal contribution of that activity to events in the external world. We define this temporal adjustment as projected delay and measure it in the macaque inferotemporal cortex using optogenetic stimulation and behavior. Two rhesus macaques performed a cortical perturbation detection task in which a visual masker appeared at different times relative to stimulation. Detection was selectively impaired when the masker began 200 ms before stimulation. We then tested this timing using Perceptography, a method that optimizes image perturbations to mimic stimulation-evoked visual events. Image perturbations presented 200 ms before stimulation elicited higher false-alarm rates than perturbations presented at stimulation onset. Here, we show that stimulation-evoked visual events in inferotemporal cortex depend preferentially on visual information originating approximately 200 ms before the cortical perturbation. This projected delay exceeds typical inferotemporal response latencies and suggests temporally extended readout mechanisms relevant to causal models of visual perception and the timing of cortical visual prostheses.

papers.title: A Computational Model Captures Orexin-Dependent Modulation of Memory Consolidation.
papers.abstract: Hippocampal sharp-wave ripple (SWR) events occur during post-experience rest and sleep and play a significant role in memory consolidation. Recent ex vivo studies have found orexin-driven neuromodulatory effects on SWR parameters and proposed that they can influence memory consolidation. Additionally, behavioral studies demonstrate contradictory results regarding orexinergic effects on memory acquisition depending on task structure and intervention time. This inconsistency, along with the diffuse spread of orexin receptors (OXR) in the CA1 and CA3 hippocampus, challenges theoretical interpretation of orexinergic effects on memory. To reconcile this problem, we propose a rate-based model linking orexinergic tone-dependent SWR statistics to memory performance. The model combines an encoding module whose gain scales with the global orexinergic tone with a consolidation module driven by OX2R-specific replay dynamics. The model is based on a plasticity rule that considers SWR events as the unit of induction. Therefore, weight change requires sufficient replay content and depolarizing drive. We observed that, depending on the task structure, encoding-dominant learning benefits discrimination as the orexin drive increases. Consolidation-dominant learning shows a non-monotonic relationship with an internal optimum level of orexinergic tone. This interaction highlights that stronger truncation at higher receptor engagement shortens memory replay and reduces the efficacy of the consolidation process. The model predicts that the optimal regime depends on task complexity reflected in sequence length. Together, these results demonstrate how task demands determine whether increased orexinergic drive enhances or impairs effective consolidation and SWR-dependent replay in the hippocampus.

papers.title: A Bayesian approach to volumetric analysis in rare neurodegenerative disorders
papers.abstract: Identifying regional brain atrophy is critical for understanding neurodegenerative disorders. Traditionally, group comparisons rely on frequentist statistics, utilising $p$-values and point estimates that offer limited characterization of uncertainty. Bayesian methods provide an alternative by estimating effect sizes and credible intervals while incorporating prior knowledge and uncertainty. This study evaluated the feasibility of Bayesian hierarchical modelling to assess regional brain atrophy in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) and Corticobasal Syndrome (CBS) compared to healthy controls. Participants meeting diagnostic criteria for CBS or PSP, together with healthy controls, were recruited from the Cambridge Centre for Parkinson-plus. Grey matter volume, cortical thickness, and subcortical volumes were derived using FreeSurfer for 210 cortical and 36 subcortical regions defined by the Human Brainnetome Atlas. Participants with PSP were classified into Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS), corticobasal syndrome variant (PSP-CBS), frontal variant (PSP-F), and other presentations (PSP-Other). Bayesian hierarchical ANOVA models with appropriate priors were used to estimate group differences. Regions of practical equivalence (ROPE) were calculated to assess evidence of meaningful group effects. A total of 428 people were included (113 PSP-RS, 30 PSP-CBS, 23 PSP-Other, 19 PSP-F, 81 CBS, and 162 healthy controls). For grey matter volume, there was evidence of whole brain volume loss compared to controls for all disease groups except PSP-Other, which showed evidence of no difference. For cortical thickness, there was evidence of global cortical thinning in CBS compared to controls, but for no other group. For subcortical volume all groups showed evidence of volume loss compared to controls. Patterns of regional atrophy were identified in keeping with previous literature, with the largest effect observed in the left pre-motor thalamus (30% reduction in CBS). There was greater loss of subcortical volume in PSP-RS compared to other PSP subgroups. Bayesian hierarchical modelling provides a feasible framework for quantifying regional brain atrophy, with interpretable effect size estimates and uncertainty measures. This approach complements conventional statistical methods, particularly in the assessment of rare neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders.

papers.title: ASC specks and α-synuclein amplify microglial NLRP3 inflammasome activation and co-localize with Lewy body pathology
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of several chronic neurodegenerative disorders, including Parkinson's disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies, and is closely associated with microglial activation. The inflammasome adaptor protein apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a caspase activation and recruitment domain (ASC) undergoes oligomerization upon inflammasome activation, resulting in the formation of ASC specks. These structures are recognized by microglia as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), thereby promoting inflammatory signaling. Recent studies have demonstrated that extracellular ASC specks associate with amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}), and that uptake of ASC-A{beta} composites by microglia amplifies pro-inflammatory responses. Although ASC specks have also been shown to potentiate -synuclein (Syn) preformed fibril-induced pathology, their interaction with monomeric Syn and their effects on inflammasome activation remain poorly understood. Here, we co-stimulated murine SIM-A9 microglia with ASC-Syn assemblies and evaluated their effects on NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Electron microscopy revealed a close association between ASC fibrils and Syn monomers. Exposure of microglia to ASC-Syn enhanced NLRP3 inflammasome activation, as evidenced by increased ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activation, and secretion of IL-1{beta} and IL-18, when compared to ASC or Syn alone. In addition, immunohistochemical analyses of post mortem brain tissue from patients with dementia with Lewy bodies demonstrated ASC expression in regions exhibiting Syn pathology and showed ASC co-localization with Syn within Lewy bodies. Collectively, these findings identify ASC-Syn assemblies as potent amplifiers of NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and suggest a mechanism through which they may contribute to sustained neuroinflammation in synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Encephalitic alphavirus infection reduces neurite outgrowth and downregulates Rho GTPase pathways in human iPSC-derived neurospheres
papers.abstract: Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) is a re-emerging neurotropic arbovirus, which affects the developing human brain, potentially leading to miscarriage, stillbirth, or long-term neurological sequelae. Currently, the mechanisms underlying these sequelae remain largely elusive. Using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurospheres as a model for brain development, we show that both human neurons and glial cells are susceptible to VEEV infection. Microscopy-based quantification reveals that VEEV impairs neurite outgrowth in the human neurospheres. To mechanistically assess these observations, we performed multi-omics analyses of VEEV-infected neurospheres and demonstrate translational shutoff including downregulation of Rho GTPase pathways. The transcriptional and proteome profile is indicative of reduced actin cytoskeleton dynamics and consequently migratory defects of cells in the neurospheres. Shotgun secretomics moreover revealed downmodulation of neurite outgrowth associated proteins including midkine (MDK), amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP) and microtubule-associated protein 1B (MAP1B). Our findings reveal mechanistic insights into how VEEV infection impairs neuronal development and demonstrate that neurospheres are a powerful platform for assessing teratogenic effects of viruses on brain development.

papers.title: Sex Differences in Human Subcortical Anatomy are Robust and Replicable in Adulthood, Already Evident Prepubertally, and Aligned with Sex Chromosomal and Gonadal Influences
papers.abstract: The existence and mechanistic bases of sex effects on human subcortical anatomy remain unclear. To address these gaps, we combined structural neuroimaging of sex differences in subcortical volume and shape across three independent cohorts (combined N=2,886) with neuroimaging maps of sex chromosomal and endocrine effects from three clinical cohorts (combined N=313, including sex chromosome aneuploidies and isolated gonadotropin-releasing hormone deficiency). We found that human subcortical anatomy shows focal sex differences of moderate-strong effect size during young adulthood (male-biased surface area overlying lateral/ventral putamen and pallidum, nucleus accumbens, ventral posterior complex of thalamus, anterior hippocampus, and medial and central nuclei of amygdala; female-biased surface area overlying caudate head, posterior/dorsal pallidum, mediodorsal, lateral dorsal, lateral geniculate, and medial geniculate nuclei of thalamus, posterior hippocampus, and basolateral and lateral nuclei of amygdala). These regional sex differences show strong within-sample reproducibility at modest sample sizes (N[≥]200) and are replicable in a fully independent mid-adulthood cohort. Adult subcortical sex differences are already evident in nascent form by pre/early puberty (age 9 years), and the same holds for cortical sex differences. Comparison with neuroimaging data from rare disorder cohorts reveals a statistically significant spatial and directional congruence of subcortical sex differences with the anatomical effects of X-chromosome dosage in the striatum and effects of testicular hormones in the amygdala. Our findings provide a reference map for the fine-grained spatial patterning of sex differences in adult subcortical shape, demonstrating its replicability, establishment before pubertal progression, and spatial concordance with potentially causal sex chromosomal and gonadal effects.

papers.title: Moving object generates topographic responses in the majority of entorhinal neurons
papers.abstract: Vision is crucial in generating a complex array of responses in rodents during spatial exploration and in humans during memory tasks. These tasks involve other variables too, e.g. multisensory cues in rodents and complex memories in humans. Further, there are major differences between the medial and lateral entorhinal cortical (MEC and LEC) functional cell types. To understand the contribution of purely visual information to entorhinal responses, we presented a simple, moving vertical bar of light to head-fixed mice, without any task or reward. Surprisingly, 66% (2391/3601) of the MEC broad spiking neurons were significantly modulated by the bar position on the screen. Visual tuning in MEC had a pronounced dorsoventral topography --the tuning strength dropped from 79% in the dorsal most quartile to 40% in the ventral most quartile. Unlike major differences in spatial and other codes between MEC and LEC during free foraging experiments, LEC cells showed very similar visual tuning (392/606, 65%), including the dorso-ventral gradient in LEC5. Additionally, the majority of putative interneurons, from MEC as well as LEC, showed similar, widespread visual tuning, unlike spatial tasks. Neurons also encoded the object motion direction (naso-temporal vs. temporo-nasal visual motion) with changes in mean rate, tuning strength and/or tuning location. Such directional nature of visual tuning indicates significant history-dependence or sequence encoding. Consistently, replacing the continuous motion by randomly flashing bar of light abolished bar-tuning in two-thirds of continuous bar-tuned cells and substantially altered tuning in the rest. These results reveal the contribution of purely visual inputs in generating anatomically organized responses in the majority of entorhinal neurons. The prevalence and similarity of visual tuning across all layers of MEC as well as LEC exceeds that of other known functional cell types (like grid cells in MEC or egocentric object tuning/time-cells in LEC) during spatial navigation tasks and could be foundational in understanding entorhinal complexity.

papers.title: A network model of path control
papers.abstract: We present a network model that enables a navigating agent to shape the spatial and temporal structure of its paths through its environment. The model is inspired by the insect fan-shaped body. In it, a recurrent neural network receives an input that encodes an agent's velocity vector. Meanwhile, network activity determines the setpoint of a control loop that influences this velocity vector through motor outputs. The network thus guides future movement using memory of past movement. We illustrate how the network's dynamics determine the trajectory features it extracts to produce the setpoint. We then relate the joint dynamics of network activity and the agent's velocity vector to the structure of the resulting paths. This network can produce paths suitable for different forms of exploration. It can also stabilize movements initiated by lower-level systems. Our analyses illustrate how recurrent neural dynamics and memory can shape behavior when embedded in closed loops.

papers.title: Learning Interpretable Switching Dynamics in Shared Neural-Behavioral Latent Space
papers.abstract: Modern recording technologies enable simultaneous measurement of high-dimensional neural activity and rich behavioral variables, creating both an opportunity and a modeling challenge: identifying the shared latent structure that mediates the brain-behavior relationship and the underlying dynamics through which it evolves across behavioral states. Existing approaches focus on different parts of this challenge: shared representation learning methods identify neural-behavioral subspaces but typically do not model dynamical structure, while dynamical models capture temporal variation and discrete state transitions in neural activity, but do not explicitly disentangle shared neural-behavioral structure from modality-specific variability. We introduce Switching Shared Latent Dynamics (SSLD), a unified framework that learns a latent representation shared between neural activity and behavior and endows this shared space with nonlinear switching recurrent dynamics to reflect the hypothesis that behaviorally relevant neural representations exhibit structured dynamical changes across behavioral states. Complementary private latent variables capture modality-specific variability, providing a window into neural activity that does not directly interact with behavior. We evaluate SSLD on a simulated dataset and four diverse experimental datasets spanning species, brain regions, and recording modalities: monkey motor and premotor cortex during reaching, somatosensory cortex during a bump task, widefield calcium imaging across mouse dorsal cortex during (a) self-initiated decision-making and (b) spontaneous movements. Across all four datasets, SSLD accurately reconstructs neural and behavioral signals, recovers discrete states in the dynamics that align with experimentally defined behavioral epochs, and isolates behaviorally-relevant neural information in the shared latent while preserving private neural variability. Ablations confirm that shared representation learning, behavioral supervision, and switching dynamics each contribute to performance. SSLD offers an interpretable approach to modeling shared neural-behavioral dynamics that complements ongoing efforts toward foundation models for neuroscience.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetic properties of Ogerin and its regulation of post-ischemia signaling in mice
papers.abstract: Ogerin, a positive regulator of GPR68, reduces infarct volume and attenuates blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage post transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). These data support the potential use of Ogerin for ischemic protection. For therapeutic interventions, tissue distribution, kinetics, and brain penetration are important characteristics for a compound. For these reasons, we performed liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis of Ogerin in mice. At 3 hours following intraperitoneal (IP) injection, liver exhibited highest level of Ogerin among all major organs assessed. We further analyzed time-dependent changes in Ogerin concentration in serum following intravenous delivery. Brain Ogerin level was ~140 ng/g at 2 hour and ~0.06ng/g at 24 hours. The brain-to-serum ratio of Ogerin was ~0.6 at 5 hr. To determine the effect of Ogerin on signaling, we collected samples 24 hours after tMCAO with or without Ogerin delivered and performed Western blotting. Consistent with the diminished level of Ogerin in brain at 24 hour, tMCAO increased similar changes in phosphorylation of PKA substrates and PKC substrates in vehicle- and Ogerin-treated groups. The pharmacokinetic data suggests that Ogerin is effective mainly during acute hours after injection. This finding generates important insights on the design of effective protocol for Ogerin delivery to potentiate GPR68 function in vivo.

papers.title: Microstructural heterogeneity of white-matter aging and its age-dependent coupling to cognition
papers.abstract: Brain white matter (WM) microstructure undergoes extensive changes with age, yet the regional and cellular heterogeneity of age-related WM alterations and their impact on cognition remain unclear. Leveraging Neurite Orientation Dispersion and Density Imaging (NODDI), an advanced microstructural modelling to capture specific WM cellular properties, we investigated age-dependent relationships between advanced microstructural markers and cognitive performance, indexed by six cognitive domains derived from principal component analysis. Using a suite of standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and NODDI techniques in eighty-six cognitively normal adults (Young: n=33, Older: n=53), we show that age group differences are widespread across whole brain white matter, with converging region-based and voxel-level evidence implicating commissural, association, and limbic pathways. Older adults exhibited significant and widespread reductions in global fractional anisotropy (FA) and neurite density index (NDI), concomitant with increases in mean diffusivity (MD), orientation density index (ODI), and free water fraction (FWF). Critically, age moderated WM-cognition associations in a domain- and tract-specific manner: younger adults exhibited stronger coupling between commissural and association tract microstructure and language and visual memory, whereas older adults showed greater dependence on projection and limbic tracts for executive and language function. The observed age-dependent coupling between specific microstructural metrics and cognition underscores the value of advanced diffusion models for capturing heterogeneity in brain aging, reveals age-specific biomarkers of cognitive health. These patterns align with phylogenetic and ontogenetic patterns of white matter vulnerability in callosal, long-range association, and limbic pathways, and suggest cellular specificity in white matter changes associated with cognitive decline.

papers.title: Lateral recurrence dynamically refines visual representations for task performance
papers.abstract: Recurrent connections are pervasive in visual cortex, and visual representations evolve as recurrent processing unfolds. Yet the mechanism underlying this temporal transformation remains poorly understood. To address this question, we trained recurrent convolutional networks on face and object recognition and tested them on a parametric stimulus set in which category, identity, and pose were systematically varied. This design isolates how lateral recurrence reshapes neural-population representational geometry and single-unit tuning across recurrent timesteps. Within the trained domain, recurrence increased the separability between identities in deeper layers, while leaving the non-trained domain representations largely unchanged. Gating lateral weights abolished the across-timestep gain in trained-domain identity decoding, demonstrating that lateral recurrence drives this refinement. At the single-unit level, recurrence strengthened the correlation between each unit's category preference and its within-domain identity sensitivity, providing a unit-level mechanism for the population-level changes. These results identify lateral recurrence as a dynamic mechanism for refining learned representational structure within a fixed neural population, yielding testable predictions for time-resolved recordings in domain-selective cortex.

papers.title: Neuronal sex identity shapes social buffering of defensive freezing behaviour in fruit flies
papers.abstract: Sex differences are pervasive across the animal kingdom1,2, shaped by reproductive strategies, ecological roles, and physiological demands. Neurobiological studies have largely focused on sex differences in reproduction and aggression3,4, leaving understudied how sex shapes other survival-relevant behaviours such as responses to predatory threats. Previous work in vertebrates uncovered sex differences in individual defence responses deployed by rats5 and in social modulation of freezing responses in zebrafish6. The origin of these differences and their potential underlying neuronal circuitry remain however unknown. Here we characterise defensive responses to a visual threat of female and male fruit flies tested alone and in groups. Individually, defensive responses are comparable across sex, with similar freezing levels and moderately increased escape responses in males. In groups, however, we uncovered strong sex differences in freezing as males show consistently shorter freezing bouts, reflecting a stronger social buffering effect than in females. Using a generalised linear mixed model, we demonstrate that the shorter freezes of male flies, when tested in groups, are not explained by well-known locomotor differences between sexes7,8. Although males move more and faster, generating stronger social motion cues that mediate the "safety in numbers" effect in female flies9,10, their response to the surrounding motion is not increased. We further identify the nervous system as the source of this sex-dimorphic behaviour by feminising males through pan-neuronal ectopic expression of transformer, a key regulator of the cell-autonomous sex-differentiation pathway. Finally, we ruled out the visual projection neurons, lobula columnar neurons 11 (LC11), detectors of social motion10, as the source of the neuronal-sex differences observed. This study identifies a neuronal origin of sex differences in socially modulated behaviour that extends beyond sex-specific behavioural modules or locomotor function, important to understand differential impact on survival upon threat across sexes.

papers.title: Neuron types and distribution of a Drosophila driver line collection
papers.abstract: Cell type designations label uniquely-identifiable groups of related cells that typically function in similar ways. Cell types divide the Drosophila melanogaster central nervous system into functional units, but remain challenging to target and identify. Previously we generated a driver line and image resource for targeting many neuron types (Meissner et al., 2025). Here we improve on identifying the targeted neurons by automated searching against electron microscopy datasets and manual scoring of search results to add 6,368 annotations across 1,772 driver lines in the collection. These annotations provide a potential training resource for future search algorithms. We then estimate the number of cell types and thus the fraction of the central nervous system labeled by the collection as a whole.

papers.title: Projection-defined ventral tegmental area neurons exhibit distinct molecular adaptations during acute fentanyl withdrawal
papers.abstract: Opioid use disorder (OUD) remains a major public health concern, with potent synthetic opioids driving overdose deaths. Understanding how synthetic opioids like fentanyl alter brain circuits to promote persistent use is critical for advancing OUD treatment. The ventral tegmental area (VTA), which projects to several other brain regions including prefrontal cortex (PFC), nucleus accumbens (NAc) and amygdala (Amy), contributes to both the euphoric and dysphoric phases of OUD. Projection target influences the baseline properties and opioid-induced neuroadaptations of VTA neurons, yet less is known about the molecular adaptations that occur across distinct VTA projections during spontaneous opioid withdrawal. Here, we investigated transcriptional responses to acute spontaneous fentanyl withdrawal in projection-defined VTA neurons. Following chronic fentanyl exposure and 24h of spontaneous withdrawal in male and female mice, we sequenced ribosome-associated RNA from VTA neurons projecting to PFC, NAc, or Amy. We found that fentanyl withdrawal produced divergent transcriptional adaptations in VTA neurons projecting to PFC compared with VTA-NAc and VTA-Amy neurons, whereas adaptations in VTA-NAc and VTA-Amy neurons were more concordant. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified fentanyl-responsive modules across VTA projections, with gene ontology analysis linking these modules to distinct biological processes. We further used regulatory enrichment analysis to identify candidate transcriptional regulators associated with fentanyl-responsive co-expression modules. Together, our data demonstrate that VTA neurons undergo distinct molecular adaptations during fentanyl withdrawal based on their projection target, providing new insight into molecular mechanisms relevant to OUD.

papers.title: An AI-Enabled Translational Drug Discovery Framework for NALCN Channelopathy: From High-Throughput Screening to Therapeutic Candidate
papers.abstract: Background: More than 90% of rare diseases lack an approved therapy, partly reflecting economic barriers in developing treatments for small patient populations. A common bottleneck is costly and resource-intensive hit-to-lead prioritization. Congenital contractures of the limbs and face, hypotonia, and developmental delay (CLIFAHDD) is an ultra-rare neurodevelopmental disease often caused by de novo gain-of-function variants in the sodium leak channel NALCN, with no approved treatments. Methods: We developed a cost and resource-efficient, AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic high-throughput screening (HTS), structural biology foundation models for hit-to-lead prioritization, and orthogonal experimental validation. We applied this framework for drug repurposing to identify NALCN inhibitors as therapeutic candidates for CLIFAHDD. We screened ~1,200 approved drugs using a fluorescence-based membrane potential assay in doxycycline-inducible HEK293 cells stably expressing the NALCN channelosome. Boltz-2 modeling predicted binding affinity and mode to prioritize hits. Lead repurposing candidates were selected by a multidisciplinary expert review panel. Lead candidates were evaluated using patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells expressing wild-type or CLIFAHDD-associated NALCN variants, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and a C. elegans NALCN gain-of-function model. Results: HTS identified 11 candidate NALCN inhibitors. Boltz-2 prioritized candidates based on predicted binding affinity and predicted binding within the NALCN pore, consistent with a direct pore-blocking mechanism. Aprepitant emerged as the lead candidate after multidisciplinary evaluation based on its predicted mechanism, pharmacologic properties, blood-brain barrier penetration, established safety profile, and regulatory approval in children and adults. Patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed partial inhibition of NALCN-mediated sodium leak currents in HEK293 cells (IC50;=2.22 M), with comparable potency against Cav3.1 (IC50=1.63 M). In primary mouse hippocampal neurons, aprepitant reduced sodium leak currents, hyperpolarized resting membrane potential, and decreased spontaneous firing. Aprepitant rescued hyperlocomotor and dystonic phenotypes in a C. elegans gain-of-function NALCN model. There was notable concordance between AI-predicted hits, phenotypic screening hits, and experimental validation. Conclusion: These findings identify aprepitant as a lead therapeutic candidate for CLIFAHDD, and establish an AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic screening, structural modeling, and experimental validation for NALCN channelopathies. This scalable and resource-conscious strategy may accelerate hit-to-lead prioritization and drug discovery for rare and ultra-rare diseases lacking effective therapies.

papers.title: Information regimes in population-graph neuroimaging: cohort context and implementation-dependent evaluation sensitivity
papers.abstract: Population-graph models aggregate a query subject with an unlabeled cohort, so their reported performance can depend on the evaluation regime rather than on predictive information alone. Evaluation context has two separable axes: the visibility of the cohort during training, and the context available at inference. We study the training-time axis under a protocol fixed before analysis, on an ABIDE-I cohort of 871 subjects (20 acquisition sites). Two population-graph implementations are compared: a learned/adaptive graph (EV-GCN) and a static weighted graph (Parisot-GCN). Within each implementation the cohort, connectivity features, outer splits and training and selection rules are held fixed, and only the information available to the graph varies. The primary estimand is the implementation-by-training-context interaction: the difference between the P0-to-P1 AUC changes of the two implementations ({Delta}{Delta}AUC). Across three preselected outer splits (666, 1024, 2024) the direction is consistent and positive, with observed interaction range 0.06285-0.13090; uncertainty is assessed separately within each split by paired subject and site-cluster bootstrap resampling and is reported per split. Splits are replication units: they are not pooled and no cross-split average is reported, so the result is not a claim of invariance to arbitrary splits. These findings tie reported population-graph performance to the evaluation information regime and motivate explicit reporting of cohort visibility. The contribution is methodological: a two-axis taxonomy of information regimes, preselected cross-split evidence that the sensitivity of reported performance to cohort context depends on the implementation, and a reusable reporting checklist.

papers.title: Path Integration Promotes Flexible Navigational Decision Making
papers.abstract: Flexible decision making depends on internal representations that capture the latent structure of a task, allowing prior knowledge to be applied in novel circumstances. Spatial navigation provides a useful model for studying flexible choice behavior, because spatial location is itself a latent variable that must be inferred rather than directly perceived. Here, we trained rats on a navigation task that required them to reach the same goal via two distinct paths from different starting locations, and then return to one of the two starting locations before beginning the next trial. Some rats were trained to rely on distal visual landmarks, allowing task states to be identified from current sensory information, whereas others were trained to rely on path integration, requiring task states to be inferred from self-motion information accumulated over the preceding trajectory. Rats trained to rely on path integration acquired the task similarly to rats trained to rely on distal visual landmarks. However, reliance on path integration enhanced rats' ability to generalize their learning to novel situations, including finding the goal from an untrained starting location and adapting to a relocated goal that reversed learned choice sequences. These findings suggest that reliance on path integration promotes the acquisition and use of mental representations that capture the latent spatial structure of navigational tasks, thereby favoring flexible navigational decisions over rigid retrieval of reinforced responses. More broadly, our findings demonstrate how information available during training can shape representations learned from experience and thereby constrain the flexibility of decision making during inference.

papers.title: Social feedback structures stay/switch decision-making in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Within natural environments, different sensory stimuli can drive mutually-exclusive behaviors such as fighting, feeding, or courting. When experiencing competing cues, how do animals decide to continue executing the current behavior or to switch to a new behavior? To address this question, we developed a closed-loop behavioral paradigm that presents actively courting male Drosophila with a fictive heat stimulus, forcing the male to choose between two competing behaviors: continue courting (stay) or escape the heat (switch). By modeling the sensorimotor transformations underlying this decision process, we discovered that male flies continually evaluate social cues, including female speed and her distance, in order to make a stay/switch decision. We investigated the neural correlates of stay/switch decision-making via brain-wide calcium imaging in head-fixed male flies presented with both fictive female visual cues and heat stimuli. We built models that predicted stay/switch decisions from neural data, which revealed that activity in a small number of brain regions, including the anterior optic tubercle, predicted decision outcomes up to 4 seconds prior to stimulus onset, whereas after stimulus onset, distributed activity across the brain was correlated with the behavioral decision. Together, these results demonstrate that Drosophila continually evaluate social feedback to inform decisions about how to respond to environmental cues, and that brain activity changes prior to presentation of the environmental cue can inform upcoming decisions. Overall, this study provides new insight into the processes underlying naturalistic decision-making in Drosophila.

papers.title: Dietary magnesium supplement enhances memory through Hippo signaling
papers.abstract: Dietary magnesium (Mg2+) supplement enhances memory in mammals and Drosophila, but whether and how Mg2+ changes molecular states of neurons, remains unknown. Here we used single-cell RNA sequencing to map cell-type specific transcriptional responses to memory-enhancing dietary Mg2+. These analyses revealed changes in Hippo-pathway gene expression in memory-relevant {beta} Kenyon Cells (KCs) of the mushroom bodies. Targeted knock-down of Merlin, hippo (hpo) and warts demonstrated requirement in {beta} KCs for Mg2+-enhanced, but not baseline memory. Further study of Hippo signaling identified Yorkie (yki) transcriptional coactivator and DNA-binding partner Scalloped (sd) to be required for baseline and Mg2+-enhanced memory. Moreover, releasing Yki::Sd of inhibition from Tondu-domain containing growth inhibitor (Tgi) specifically in {beta} KCs enhanced memory, independent of diet. Analyses of Yki::Sd target genes identified several required in {beta} KCs for baseline memory, including crb and Glut1 which are also Mg2+-induced in a Hippo-dependent manner in {beta} KCs. These genes suggest that aiding the metabolic demands of long-term memory and facilitating structural neuronal plasticity are key mediators of Mg2+-induced memory enhancement. We propose pharmacological enhancement of Sd-dependent transcription, and activity of particular Sd-target genes may have therapeutic potential for memory disorders.

papers.title: Associations Between Neural Responses to Social Fairness and Financial Exploitation Vulnerability Vary With Age and Emotional Intelligence
papers.abstract: Financial exploitation often arises in social contexts in which individuals must evaluate fairness, trust, and interpersonal information during financial decisions. We examined whether neural responses to fairness in social versus nonsocial contexts relate to financial exploitation vulnerability and whether these relationships vary with age, emotional intelligence, and affect. A total of 310 adults spanning ages 21-89 completed an fMRI Ultimatum Game in which they accepted or rejected offers from human and computer partners, along with measures of financial exploitation vulnerability, emotional intelligence, and affect. Participants were strongly sensitive to offer fairness, and individual differences in behavioral sensitivity to partner type were associated with social-relative anterior insula responses to unfairness. Greater baseline negative affect was associated with stronger anterior insula differentiation between social and nonsocial fairness. Financial exploitation vulnerability was associated with prefrontal responses to social-relative fairness in ways that depended on individual characteristics: age moderated its association with dorsomedial prefrontal cortex activation, whereas emotional intelligence moderated its association with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation. Whole-brain connectivity analyses further showed that age moderated associations between emotional intelligence and executive control network connectivity with posterior cingulate and right temporoparietal regions. These findings suggest that vulnerability to financial exploitation is reflected in how social context is integrated with affective and individual characteristics across adulthood.

papers.title: Motivational incentives improve working memory performance by enhancing memory-based representations rather than altering response strategies
papers.abstract: Motivational incentives are known to improve working memory (WM) when items differ in value, but whether they enhance performance when all items are equally valued, and if so, by what mechanism, remains unclear. Improvements could reflect enhanced memory-based representations or speed-accuracy trade-offs, whereby incentives promote slower, more cautious responding without improving memory itself. Here, we tested these alternatives across two experiments using an auditory WM task in which incentives varied across trials, but all items on a trial were equally incentivised. In Experiment 1,we allowed participants to resubmit their responses if desired. Reward-related improvements in WM performance were selectively observed when memory load was high, and only at serial positions associated with greater interference. These improvements were also dissociated from systematic response slowing and resubmission behaviour. This indicated that the benefits of incentives were unlikely to be attributable to response caution. Critically, in Experiment 2, motivational benefits persisted under strict response deadlines, where speed cannot be traded for accuracy. Computational modelling showed that reward selectively improved the precision of memory-based responses without reducing guessing. Together, these findings indicate that motivational incentives improve WM by enhancing the quality of memory-based representations, rather than by strategic slowing or altering response strategies.

papers.title: Direction-sensitive neural correlates of voluntary pain regulation: regional response attenuation during down-regulation and exploratory prefrontal-valuation coupling
papers.abstract: Voluntary cognitive regulation can increase or decrease pain, but direction-sensitive neural correlates may emerge at different analytical levels. We reanalyzed 3,201 thermal-stimulation trials from 33 participants, integrating 0-200 warmth/pain ratings, regional fMRI activity, and trial-wise lagged coupling. Both instructions shifted ratings in the intended direction, with no reliable difference in mean success. Down-regulation was associated with lower bilateral S2/opercular and insular activity and higher left dlPFC/IFJ activity after FDR correction across 32 regions; run-matched comparisons were weaker and none survived the corresponding correction. Contrast-map Neurologic Pain Signature attenuation did not replicate in a rating-adjusted FWL-LSS trial-wise analysis despite strong temperature sensitivity. Up-regulation success covaried with an exploratory, post selection lagged dlPFC/IFJ-valuation composite (r = -0.546, 95% CI [-0.764, -0.270]). The association exceeded matched reverse-direction, zero-lag, and time-reversed controls, lay outside permutation and circular-shift nulls, and persisted after AR(1) prewhitening. A transition-level analysis across 297 up-regulation transitions preserved a negative success-by-source interaction (adjusted three-target mean beta = -0.163, cluster-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.290, -0.054], Freedman-Lane p = 0.010). Six session-wise DCM variants showed no consistent regulation-versus-passive effective-connectivity effect and did not independently validate an up-specific directed mechanism. These analyses identify a down-regulation-associated regional pattern and a candidate prefrontal-valuation coupling association requiring independent confirmation.

papers.title: Self-Exciting Population Event Models Reveal Abnormal Temporal Amplification in MAPT-Mutant Human Brain Assembloids
papers.abstract: Human brain assembloids provide a tractable platform for studying mutation-specific network dysfunction, but most studies do not distinguish whether abnormal activity arises from increased spontaneous initiation or stronger history-dependent amplification. We introduce a low-dimensional discrete-time self-exciting population model for calcium-imaging event sequences that separates baseline initiation (%[mu]), integrated history-dependent gain (%[eta]), and memory decay (%[tau]). Across 175 recordings from 13 MAPT p.R406W or CRISPR-corrected isogenic assembloids, biological-unit inference identified a 4.31-fold increase in %[eta] in mutants (95% CI 3.20- 5.84; exact p=7.8x10-4), without increased baseline activity. Parametric predictive checks exposed residual Poisson overdispersion; fixed-decay and beta-binomial sensitivity analyses nevertheless preserved the mutant history effect. Median %[eta] separated all 13 held-out assembloids, while a multifeature recording-level RBF-SVM achieved AUC 0.816 under nested whole-assembloid holdout. These results identify robust history-dependent temporal amplification as a functional MAPT-mutant network phenotype.

papers.title: Flexible 3D multimodal organoid interface reveals functional subnetworks and coordinated circuit activity in cortical organoids
papers.abstract: The balance between excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) neurons is fundamental to cortical function, and its disruption underlies a wide range of neurological disorders, including epilepsy, Alzheimers disease and autism spectrum disorder. Cortical organoids offer a promising model to study this balance, as they recapitulate key features of brain development, including the emergence of E/I circuitry. However, no existing technology can simultaneously resolve neuronal identity, spatial organization, and dynamic network activity within intact organoids, limiting precise interrogation of E/I circuit function. Here, we report INFORM, an INtegrated Flexible Organoid Recording Multimodal neural interface that conformally wraps organoids of any size and shape, enabling long-term recordings over 371 days with above 90% of channels detecting spikes. INFORM interface combines four distinct modalities; electrophysiology, two-photon calcium imaging, targeted electrical microstimulation, and chemical intervention to monitor and modulate neural activity across multiple spatial and temporal scales spanning from action potentials from single neurons to synchronized bursts from large-scale populations. Such high-resolution interrogation enables probing of emergence of functional connectivity in fusing assembloids and resolves spatially discrete functional subnetworks that can be selectively recruited and modulated by INFORM. Neurotransmission blockade confirms that stimulus-evoked suppression of neuronal spiking is mediated by GABAergic inputs providing direct functional evidence of the presence of inhibitory signaling in organoids. This work allows single-cell dissection of functional networks in brain organoids, providing a powerful platform for modelling and studying cortical development, neurological diseases, and the E/I imbalances underlying circuit dysfunction.

papers.title: Neural circuit mechanisms for multi-tasking
papers.abstract: Neural activity during performance of a cognitive or motor task is often described as lying on a low-dimensional manifold in the space of all possible activity patterns. When multiple tasks are performed, an individual brain region's activity may generate multiple such manifolds. Several models have been introduced to explain this capability, each with different assumptions concerning architecture and inputs. Here, we develop a theory of multi-tasking according to which models and experimental paradigms can be organized. We introduce a distinction between sequential and simultaneous multi-tasking, the performance of one task at a time or multiple in parallel. We show that interference between tasks often prevents multi-tasking and introduce a model of ``task barcodes" that circumvents this problem and parameterizes a neuronal population's task selectivity. Our theory reveals categorical distinctions between neural circuit mechanisms supporting multi-tasking that can be probed using physiological recordings.

papers.title: LLM-powered automatic scoring tools for memory recall
papers.abstract: Free recall of naturalistic stimuli, such as films and stories, reveals what people remember and how they organize it. Scoring such recall requires matching each recalled utterance to the encoded stimulus, and doing this manually often makes large studies impractical. Existing automated methods mostly return similarity or aggregate scores rather than explicit matches between recalled and stimulus content. Here we introduce an open-source, model-agnostic pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to divide the stimulus and the recall into information units and to match units between the two texts. The output is a table of unit-to-unit matches with accuracy labels, from which standard analysis scripts compute recall measures. We validated the pipeline with four LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT 5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 2.5 Flash) on three datasets. On typed recall of four short stories, agreement between each model and two trained raters ({phi} = .73-.79) was close to the agreement between the raters themselves ({phi} = .77). A second run reproduced each model's matches ({phi} = .91-.97) more closely than the raters agreed with each other. On spoken recall of 10 films, every model attributed recall to the correct film with high agreement. On uncorrected speech-to-text recall of a television episode, agreement varied more across models. The median cost was under $1 per participant for every model. These results suggest that the pipeline can serve as a reliable, low-cost alternative to manual scoring of free recall.

papers.title: Huntingtin and Celsr3 Orchestrate Spontaneous Long-Distance Spinal Cord Regeneration
papers.abstract: Spontaneous spinal cord regeneration is an endogenous process operational in diverse vertebrate and select mammalian species. Yet despite resulting in functional regeneration, axonal regrowth dynamics as well as underlying molecular programs are largely unknown. Live-cell imaging following laser axotomy of individual zebrafish spinal cord M-cell axons reveals a time-sensitive multistep process. From a genetic screen we uncover previously unrecognized roles for two evolutionary conserved genes, celsr3 and huntingtin (htt) in spontaneous spinal cord regeneration. Specifically, we find that htt is critical to initiate a transcriptional injury response in regenerating M-cells, enabling their axon to traverse the injury site. Once axons cross the injury site celsr3 functions to increase growth rates, while both celsr3 and htt function to sustain long-range axonal growth. Moreover, we show that htt is dispensable for optic nerve and peripheral motor neuron regeneration, and that reducing soma-to-injury site distance in htt mutant M-cell axons partially restores regeneration, demonstrating a selective role in long-range CNS axon regeneration. Consistent with a transport-based mechanism, genetic knockdown of htt-associated axonal transport proteins recapitulates the htt mutant regeneration phenotype. Combined, our results provide compelling evidence for a time and distance-sensitive multistep molecular framework in which celsr3 dependent growth rate modulation and htt dependent axonal transport promote spontaneous, long-range spinal cord regeneration.
